citizen.blurb: The language engine behind tools like ChatGPT — trained on enormous amounts of text.
citizen.standfirst: What 'large' actually measures, why a bigger model writes better without getting more honest, and what that means for picking one.
citizen.core:
A large language model is the kind of AI behind many chatbots. It predicts what text should come next, but at a huge scale. It can have billions of tuned settings called parameters, learned from large amounts of text.

A common mix-up is that "large" means how much a model can remember in a chat. It doesn't. That is the context window. "Large" refers to how many parameters the model has. This number stays fixed after training.

Size can also change what a model can do. A small model may handle simple text. A much larger one may follow complex instructions, write code, or solve harder tasks. Some of these skills appear as models grow, rather than being taught one by one.
citizen.everyday:
You've probably used a large language model already. ChatGPT and Claude are built around them. You type a question, and the model creates a natural-sounding reply.

Larger models often follow complex instructions better and write more consistent answers. But they can still be wrong while sounding confident. Good writing does not mean the facts are correct. Check important claims, especially names, dates, and laws.
citizen.businesses:
Model size is a trade-off. Large models handle vague or difficult tasks better, but they also cost more and can be slower.

Many companies use a mix: a large model for hard questions and a smaller, cheaper model for simple tasks.

Large models can also be hard to inspect. You cannot trace billions of parameters like normal software rules. So companies often test the model's outputs and add guardrails around it.
citizen.appBuilders:
Bigger models often follow hard instructions and reason better, but they also cost more and respond more slowly.

For narrow tasks, such as sorting support tickets, a smaller model may work almost as well for much less money. Test smaller models first using real examples from the task.
citizen.modelBuilders:
Models often improve when parameters, training data, and computing power grow together. Researchers call this a scaling law.

But size alone is not enough. A model also needs enough training data. Growing parameters without enough data can waste computing power and money.
citizen.smalltalk: A large language model is a language model scaled up to billions of parameters and trained on huge amounts of text. That size can unlock abilities smaller models lack, but it also makes the model more costly to build and run.

technical.blurb: A transformer scaled to billions or trillions of parameters, where scaling laws and emergent abilities drive most of the capability gain.
technical.standfirst: Compute-optimal scaling, the Chinchilla result, emergent abilities, and the cost and deployment trade-offs of training and serving a model at this scale.
technical.core:
A large language model (LLM) is a transformer-based neural network trained on next-token prediction at a scale where parameter count runs from several billion up into the trillions. The architecture underneath usually stays the same across model sizes; parameter count, training data volume, and training compute are what actually change from one large language model to the next.

More parameters does not automatically mean a better model. Research behind the Chinchilla scaling paper found that many early large language models were significantly undertrained for their size, holding far more parameters than their training data could justify. Compute-optimal training scales training tokens roughly in step with parameter count. A smaller model trained on proportionally more data can outperform a larger, undertrained one at the same compute budget.

Capability doesn't grow linearly with scale, which is what makes the cost worth pursuing. Certain abilities, multi-step reasoning and few-shot in-context learning, show up unevenly across scale. They're barely present in smaller models, then reliably present past some threshold, with no architectural change causing the jump.
technical.appBuilders:
Model size functions as a cost-versus-capability dial, and it's a separate axis from context window, which is a deployment-time setting. Larger models generally handle ambiguous instructions and long reasoning chains more reliably, but every added billion parameters increases both per-token latency and inference cost, since a forward pass touches the full parameter set regardless of how simple the input is.

For narrow, well-specified tasks such as classification and extraction, a smaller model often reaches near-parity with a much larger one. Benchmark task-specific accuracy against cost before defaulting to the largest tier. Quantization and distillation are the standard levers for shrinking a large language model's footprint once you've picked the smallest size that clears your accuracy bar.
technical.businesses:
Deploying a large language model means budgeting for inference cost that scales with usage volume and model size simultaneously, which makes model selection a recurring cost decision. Vendor API pricing usually tiers by model size, and self-hosting only becomes economical at volumes high enough to justify the GPU infrastructure and the engineering to run it reliably.

Governance is harder at this scale because the model can't be audited line by line the way a smaller rules-based system can. Most serious deployments rely on output-level evaluation, held-out test sets, and red-teaming for failure modes. Licensing terms also vary sharply between providers, closed API-only models, openly released weights, and restricted "open" licenses, which affects whether internal fine-tuning or on-premises deployment is even an option. A regulated industry evaluating a vendor's large language model usually needs answers to both questions before signing anything: what the model was trained on, and who can see the prompts sent to it.
technical.modelBuilders: Training a frontier-scale large language model means distributed training across thousands of accelerators, splitting the model and data across GPUs or TPUs using techniques like tensor and pipeline parallelism, since a model this size doesn't fit in a single device's memory. Training runs at this scale can cost tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in compute alone. Scaling laws matter operationally because they let a team estimate the loss a target model size and data volume will reach before committing to the run.
technical.smalltalk: A large language model is a transformer scaled to billions or trillions of parameters. Training data has to scale with it too, or the extra parameters go to waste. Past a certain scale, new abilities show up that smaller versions don't have.
